You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make her close her jacket fully
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is the woman's jacket fully closed, with its front panels brought together and no visible opening remaining along the closure?
node.criteria: Pass if visual evidence establishes that the jacket's front panels are brought together along the entire closure with no remaining opening. Fail if a genuine opening between the front closure edges is visible, including a partly closed jacket. Identify the closure edges rather than treating the outer silhouette, loose fabric, folds, or sideways pose as an opening by themselves. Unknown if occlusion, motion blur, viewing angle, or image resolution prevents establishing whether the closure is complete. A pose change or reduced apparent gap alone does not satisfy this condition.
node.binding: Judge the woman's jacket in the image against the requested fully closed state. Use the woman's jacket in the SOURCE image as the reference garment and inspect its front closure in the EDITED image.

node_traces.evidence: In the edited image, the woman is turned sideways and the pink jacket hangs open, with a broad visible gap between the front panels. The closure is not fully closed.

response.content: {"text":"The trace is valid and fully queried, with no transport, schema, or dependency failure; the disagreement is semantic. The edited image shows the woman turned sideways and the pink jacket flaring outward, but that silhouette alone does not establish a gap between the actual front closure edges. The node’s evidence asserts a broad opening without identifying those edges or distinguishing open closure from loose fabric and pose, despite its criteria requiring that distinction. Tighten the binding to compare the source garment with the edited image and require evidence about the closure itself; use unresolved when the angle or occlusion prevents judging it. The reference label constrains the aggregate, but is not atomic ground truth: investigate whether the apparent opening is genuine rather than forcing a yes. High confidence in the current unsupported interpretation is a reason to improve evidence grounding, not to lower the completion standard."}
